nameStory: Atlantic ivy gets its name from its native range along the Atlantic coasts of Europe, particularly Ireland where it's also called Irish ivy. The word 'ivy' comes from the Old English 'ifig,' referring to these climbing, clinging plants that seem to embrace whatever they grow on.
description: Atlantic ivy is a vigorous evergreen vine that climbs walls, trees, and fences using tiny rootlets along its stems. It can grow quite large, reaching 30 feet or more as it scrambles up surfaces or spreads across the ground as a dense carpet. The glossy, dark green leaves are typically larger than those of common ivy, often with 3-5 broad lobes when young, becoming more oval-shaped on flowering stems. This non-native plant has escaped cultivation and can be found growing wild in some New England areas.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Glossy, leathery leaves that are noticeably larger than common ivy, often 2-4 inches across with 3-5 broad, shallow lobes. The leaves feel thick and waxy to the touch, staying green year-round.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Climbs vigorously using small aerial rootlets that you can see and feel along the stems, creating a fuzzy texture on the climbing side. Also spreads as dense groundcover in shade.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small, yellowish-green flowers appear in rounded clusters only on mature plants, usually high up on climbing stems. The flowers have 5 tiny petals and bloom in fall.

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Dark blue-black berries about the size of small peas appear in winter, arranged in rounded clusters. The berries feel firm and have a waxy coating.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Woody stems become quite thick with age, covered in small rootlets on the side touching the climbing surface. Young stems are green and flexible.

habitat: Atlantic ivy thrives in disturbed areas, abandoned lots, and edges of woodlands where it has escaped from gardens. It prefers partial shade but tolerates full sun, growing in various soil types from rich garden soil to rocky areas. You'll often find it climbing old stone walls, abandoned buildings, and large trees in suburban and urban areas.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as bright green shoots, and the evergreen leaves provide consistent identification. This is when the vine puts on its most vigorous growth.
seasonality.summer: Mature leaves are at their glossiest, and the plant continues climbing and spreading. The contrast between younger, more lobed leaves and older oval leaves is most apparent.
seasonality.fall: Mature plants produce small yellowish-green flower clusters, though these are often high up and hard to spot. The evergreen foliage remains unchanged while deciduous plants around it drop leaves.
seasonality.winter: Dark berries ripen and persist into winter, and the evergreen leaves make this one of the few green climbing plants visible. Snow often clings to the dense foliage.

funFact: Atlantic ivy can live for hundreds of years and eventually develop tree-like trunks over a foot thick - some ancient specimens in Europe are so massive they've been mistaken for trees rather than vines!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with common ivy (English ivy), but Atlantic ivy has noticeably larger, broader leaves that feel thicker and more leathery. Memory trick: 'Atlantic ivy has LARGE leaves' - both words start with 'A' and 'L'.
contextualKnowledge: Like other non-native ivies, Atlantic ivy is considered invasive in many areas and can damage buildings and trees while crowding out native plants. Many gardeners are now removing it in favor of native climbing alternatives.
compareHints: Atlantic ivy differs from common ivy by having larger, thicker leaves and more vigorous growth. Compared to Canary Islands ivy, Atlantic ivy has smaller leaves and is more cold-hardy. Persian ivy has even larger leaves that are often heart-shaped rather than lobed.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Common ivy is by far the most widespread Hedera species in New England.
Canary Islands Ivy stands out from its relatives by its distinctly larger, thicker leaves and more robust stems.
Persian ivy stands out from its ivy relatives primarily by size - it has the largest leaves and most vigorous growth of any Hedera species.
